variants.headline: Allies join the war against {{opponent}}
body: The war against {{opponent}} is no longer ours alone. {{allies}} have answered the call of the pact between us, and what one nation carried now rests on several. Their banners move with ours from this week on.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A warning for our other rivals
body: {{allies}} have entered the war against {{opponent}} under our pact. Until a promise like that is tested, a rival can tell itself our allies would sit a war out. Now even a ruler with no stake in this fight has to reckon with the chance of facing them as well as us.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The pact answered in arms
body: We are credibly informed that the pact has been answered, and that the war against {{opponent}} now includes {{allies}} on our side. Treaties kept in hard years are the ones worth signing in calm ones, and this one has been kept. We congratulate the chancelleries on their constancy.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! We do not fight alone
body: News from the war against {{opponent}}! The pact is honored, and {{allies}} stand at our side! We do not fight alone! We do not fight alone! Carry it to every street and every gate!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Barbarians in sight of {{cityName}}
body: Scouts count {{barbarians}} barbarians in the country around {{cityName}}. The garrison has been warned, and the herds have been brought in from the outlying fields.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Raiders at the walls
body: The scouts count {{barbarians}} barbarians outside the walls! Bar your gates, mind the herds, and keep the children close! Keep the children close!

variants.headline: The herdsmen reach {{cityName}} without the herds
body: They saw the dust before the scouts did, and rode in with empty saddles. {{barbarians}} barbarians now camp within reach of {{cityName}}, and nobody walks the evening roads. The dogs know first, one of them said. The dogs are always first.

variants.headline: Counting raiders at {{cityName}}
body: The scouts agree on the number, which is rare: {{barbarians}} barbarians in the country around {{cityName}}. A band that size does not wander, it feeds, and it will burn what it cannot carry. The men who hunt it down will be men the harvest wanted first.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, the garrison answers: {{posture}}
body: It is set down that {{barbarians}} barbarians were counted in the lands of {{cityName}}, and that the command there has entered its answer in the record: {{posture}}.

variants.headline: {{city}} goes hungry under siege
body: {{city}} is under siege and running short of food. A woman boiling supper in a shared courtyard says she has started saving the cooking water. "There's a little starch in it yet. It goes in tomorrow's pot."

variants.headline: Who can still buy supper in {{city}}?
body: {{city}} is hungry under siege, and the first households to go without may be those that normally buy food a day at a time. A laundress who lives on each day's earnings has no store to run down. A few sacks still for sale at the market tell us very little about whether her children have eaten.

variants.headline: In {{city}}, the queue starts before dawn
body: Citizens of {{city}}, the siege has reached the table! The baker opens late and shuts early, and the line forms in the dark before his shutters do. When the loaf is smaller than the hand holding it, the war has come indoors.

variants.headline: To the faithful of {{city}}: hold fast
body: The city is besieged and the cupboards are bare. Keep the gates shut and the shrines open, feed a neighbor where you can, and carry what you spare to those with nothing. The trial is shared; so is the bread.

variants.headline: The walls of {{cityName}} are failing
body: The recent fighting has left the defenses of {{cityName}} at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}. More than half of what guarded the city is gone, and the gap is visible from outside the walls.

variants.headline: An accounting of {{cityName}}
body: City: {{cityName}}.
Defenses remaining: {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}.
Assessment: the greater part is gone.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight: heavy damage at {{cityName}}
body: Abroad tonight. The city of {{cityName}} has taken heavy damage in the fighting. Its defenses stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}.

variants.headline: The walls of a rival come down
body: {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, stands at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}, and walls that far gone no longer guard a city. They mark the door. Our generals have spent the campaign learning where the doors are, and this one is coming off its hinges.

variants.headline: Our forces attack before {{cityName}}
body: Our command before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, has gone over to the attack. The order that went out reads {{posture}}.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, by arithmetic
body: The front before {{cityName}} has moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and the change is not weather. It is arithmetic: officers paid to count costs have counted them, and the sum says the opening before the city is worth its price.

variants.headline: The offensive at {{cityName}}, entered
body: It is set down that our command before {{cityName}}, a city held by {{civilization}}, has passed to the assault, and that its stance is now given in the orders as {{posture}}.

variants.headline: The war moves to {{civilization}}'s streets
body: The push at {{cityName}} has begun in earnest. After the waiting and the counting, our men are going forward, and going fast. Wars are dear to finish, and the last mile of one is always paid in somebody's street.

variants.headline: Back in the fight near {{cityName}}
body: After falling back, the command near {{cityName}} has taken up a new stance against {{civilization}}: {{posture}}. The front there is active again, and our soldiers are back at the line.

variants.headline: The pullback ends at {{cityName}}
body: Our forces had fallen back from {{cityName}}. The new stance, {{posture}}, ends that. A step back followed by a step forward was never a retreat; it was a run-up, and the ground given up is now ground to take back.

variants.headline: Our forces are back at the line near {{cityName}}
body: Near {{cityName}} tonight, our forces are back at the line. The command has moved from withdrawal to {{posture}}. Officers describe the front as active again.

variants.headline: The second try at {{cityName}}
body: The orders came down, and our men are walking forward again near {{cityName}}. Two tries at the same ground means two issues of boots and bread, and it is not the council's boots on the road. Let them say what the first withdrawal bought, before they bill us for the second try.

variants.headline: The line comes back from {{cityName}}
body: Our command before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, has shifted from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The line on that front is drawing back.

variants.headline: The withdrawal before {{cityName}}
body: The front before {{cityName}} has gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}, and with it our line has moved back. Someone gave that order, for a reason, at a price, and not one of the three has been explained. The country paid for the ground. It can be told what the payment bought.

variants.headline: Letters from the front: {{cityName}}
body: Letters from the front relate that our forces before {{cityName}} have gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The news reached the printer with the evening post, short and without explanation, and he passes it on as it came.

variants.headline: The boys are off the front at {{cityName}}
body: Word came ahead of them, and the street heard it before the council did. Our men are coming off the front at {{cityName}}. Some houses here will set a place at the table again. Others will ask what the push cost, and wait longer for an answer.

variants.headline: Enemy colors near {{cityName}}
body: Soldiers flying the colors of {{enemies}} have been counted within reach of {{cityName}}. We are at war with them, and this is how close the war has come.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The enemy is near
body: Troops of {{enemies}} are sighted outside the walls! Stand to your posts, keep the watch, and leave the roads clear for the army! Leave the roads clear!

variants.headline: Three things an army near {{cityName}} can do
body: Troops of {{enemies}} stand within reach of {{cityName}}, and an army that close can do one of three things: besiege the walls, burn the fields, or pin the garrison in place while its friends strike elsewhere. Which it does depends on its strength, not its manners. That is the number to count first.

variants.headline: Enemy troops just showed up near {{cityName}}
body: The list: {{enemies}}. Every name on it is at war with us, and every one is this close. Yes, all of them.

variants.headline: {{count}} enemy units destroyed in the field
body: Our forces destroyed {{count}} enemy units in the recent fighting, every one of them belonging to the same enemy army.

variants.headline: The enemy's losses, counted
body: Enemy units destroyed by our forces: {{count}}.
Armies they came from: one.
The season's fighting, and the season's bill: theirs.

variants.headline: {{count}} enemy units destroyed in the fighting
body: From the front tonight. Our forces have destroyed {{count}} enemy units in the latest fighting. Command says every one belonged to the same army.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{count}} enemy units destroyed
body: The tally from the front is plain: {{count}} of the enemy's units destroyed by our arms! Sing it in the taverns and tell it in the streets! {{count}} of them, and the enemy knows the number too!

variants.headline: A capital falls, far from home
body: A foreign capital has fallen by conquest, {{distance}} leagues from our nearest city. The fighting never approached our borders, but the balance of powers abroad has changed all the same.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: After {{cityName}} falls, where do the envoys go?
body: {{cityName}}, the capital of {{loser}}, is now in the hands of {{winner}}. If the old government opens its offices elsewhere and the foreign envoys follow it, their change of address will tell us whose signature their governments still honor.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital
body: It is set down that {{winner}} has taken the capital of {{loser}} by force of arms, {{distance}} leagues from our own cities. The chronicles teach that providence moves in the fall of thrones, and that its meaning shows itself only later.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen
body: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen to {{winner}}. The city lies {{distance}} miles from our frontier. Observers expect the region's maps to be redrawn.

variants.headline: Peace near our borders
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have ended their war. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} leagues from our border, and the roads between them are open to carts and couriers again.

variants.headline: Neighbors at peace again
body: Word reaches us that {{initiator}} and {{target}} have laid down their arms, and that the peace asked no visible price of either side. Quiet borders make good neighbors, and ours are the quieter for it. We wish both peoples a long and dull peace, the best kind there is.

variants.headline: The quiet between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has ended with no concessions and no capitulation, which is usually an accounting: both sides had spent what they meant to spend, and neither could buy more. The quarrel closes at a loss to everyone. That is the cheapest way left to close one.

variants.headline: When the neighbors' fire burns low
body: When the neighbors' fire burns low, the whole street sleeps warmer. So it is with {{initiator}} and {{target}} at peace.

variants.headline: War breaks out near our borders
body: {{initiator}} has opened a war against {{target}}. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} leagues from our nearest city, and the war is not ours. Both of the belligerents, however, are neighbors of ours.

variants.headline: A war next door
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has opened within {{nearest}} miles of our border, and no war that close stays other people's business for long. Armies forage where they stand, and markets close where armies forage. Both sides will soon be counting what our friendship is worth, and we should set the price before they do.

variants.headline: {{initiator}} at war with {{target}}
body: War close to home tonight: a declaration by {{initiator}} against {{target}}. We are outside this fight. At a coach station here, one driver is waiting to talk to someone who has made the return trip. "I'll sell seats when I know I can bring people back."

variants.headline: Their war, our doorstep
body: Citizens, {{initiator}} and {{target}} are at war, {{nearest}} leagues from our farms! When the great quarrel, it is the small fence that gets trampled, and ours is the smallest fence hereabouts. The council should say plainly what we mean to do about it, before the answer is chosen for us.

variants.headline: A war nearby, set down
body: It is set down that {{initiator}} made war upon {{target}}, and that the nearer of the two lies {{nearest}} leagues from our lands. The entry takes no side. It notes only that the fighting is near, and that our own peace holds.

variants.headline: A capital falls near our own border
body: {{winner}} has taken a capital from {{loser}} by conquest, close enough to our border to be our concern. One neighbor has grown stronger, and another weaker.

variants.headline: What {{winner}}'s capture means here
body: A conquered capital makes {{winner}} a stronger presence on our border and {{loser}} a smaller one. Whoever holds the seat of a state holds its taxes, its roads and its treaties, and those now answer to {{winner}}. A change of that size, this close, becomes our business whatever flag flies on the walls.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital near our borders
body: In this season {{winner}} took the capital of {{loser}} by the sword. The news came swiftly, for it fell near our own marches. Our grandfathers' maps named that city under another hand, and our grandchildren's will name it under {{winner}}'s.

variants.headline: A capital just fell near us
body: {{winner}} has taken a capital from {{loser}}, and not far from us. Who got stronger today? Not us.

variants.headline: A town changes hands near our border
body: A foreign town has changed hands by conquest, {{distance}} leagues from our nearest city. Neither its old master nor its new one is us, and the fighting stayed off our soil.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: {{cityName}}, lately belonging to {{loser}}, has been taken by {{winner}}. The town lies {{distance}} miles from our nearest city, and its fields, roads and tolls now answer to another flag. Whoever collects those tolls will want a friend on the border, and we are the border.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: {{cityName}}
body: Notice to travelers and merchants. {{cityName}}, {{distance}} leagues from our cities, has passed to {{winner}} by conquest. Expect a new authority at the gate, new papers to match, and old maps to be wrong.

variants.headline: A new flag {{distance}} miles out
body: {{winner}} has taken a town from {{loser}}, {{distance}} miles from our nearest city. To the mapmakers it is a line moving. To us it is the next town over, and our border towns will be the first to meet the new neighbors across the fence.

variants.headline: {{neighbor}}'s army now outranks ours
body: The army of {{neighbor}} now outweighs ours. The border between us has not moved, and the balance of strength at it has tipped all the same.

variants.headline: The tally of arms
body: Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
The larger: theirs, and newly so.

variants.headline: Ask why {{neighbor}}'s army passed ours
body: Citizens, the army of {{neighbor}} is now the stronger, and no one in the council will say when that was allowed to happen. Ask the border sentries what they hear drilling at night. A gap left unmeasured gets measured later, in land.

variants.headline: The balance of arms has turned
body: It is set down that the host of {{neighbor}} has grown past our own in strength. The seasons turn, and the balance of arms turns with them; the scribe notes the crossing and keeps the page.

variants.headline: Our army passes {{neighbor}}'s
body: Our forces now rate ahead of {{neighbor}}'s. A farmer near the border says he has begun asking whether it is safe to turn his cattle out onto the far pasture again.

variants.headline: Our arms in good order
body: We are informed that the strength of our army now surpasses that of {{neighbor}}, an advance owing much to steady counsel and diligently kept armories. The nation may take satisfaction in a policy that has borne so visible a fruit.

variants.headline: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s
body: New count: our army outweighs {{neighbor}}'s. Windows like this don't stay open. Nobody prints the schedule.

variants.headline: The account of strength
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The larger: ours, and newly so.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes heavy damage
body: The recent fighting has done heavy harm to the walls of {{city}}, which now stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}. Masons are on the ramparts, and the bill for the mending is still being written.

variants.headline: The cost to {{city}}
body: The walls of {{city}} are down to {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}. Stone does not crack on its own. Either the garrison was thin on the day or the relief came late, and the citadel has named neither. The city is owed the truth about which one it was paying for.

variants.headline: The crack in {{city}}'s wall
body: The mason came down his ladder at noon and did not go back up. The wall he was repointing stands at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}, and by evening everyone in {{city}} could say the number by heart.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{city}}! The walls are hurt
body: The enemy has struck at the walls! They stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} and hold. Keep the watch, and mend what is broken. The walls hold at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}}!

variants.headline: Our forces counterattack at {{cityName}}
body: Our command at {{cityName}} has changed the order of the front from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The troops there have stopped absorbing blows and begun returning them.

variants.headline: From defense to the strike at {{cityName}}
body: At {{cityName}} the order has turned from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. A hedgehog only bites when the dog is tired, and the enemy at the walls looks spent. Press while the pressing is good.

variants.headline: Our forces attack at {{cityName}}
body: In {{cityName}} tonight, our forces have gone over to the attack. The order of the front has changed from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The guns are firing outward.

variants.headline: The defense holds and answers
body: Letters from {{cityName}} relate that the command there, having held fast through the order {{previousPosture}}, has now given the word {{posture}}. We are informed the change was made in good order and at the proper hour, and we find in that the marks of sound management.

variants.headline: The front at {{cityName}} goes defensive
body: Our command at {{cityName}} has changed the order of the front from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The troops there have stopped pushing outward and turned to hold what they have.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, a stance change unexplained
body: We are informed that the command at {{cityName}} has set aside the order {{previousPosture}} for {{posture}}. No reasons have been offered, and this paper's enquiries at the citadel have met with the courtesy of closed doors.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Our soldiers stand at the walls
body: Word for the town: the soldiers are coming in from the fields and standing to the walls. Keep calm. Keep the watch. Give the soldiers the road. The soldiers at the walls, and the town behind them!

variants.headline: The record of {{cityName}}'s front
body: It is set down that our forces at {{cityName}} took the order {{posture}}, having before stood at {{previousPosture}}. The change is entered without comment, the record's habit being to keep the facts and leave the judgment to the reader.

variants.headline: A war ends in capitulation
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has ended in capitulation. One of the two nations now answers to the other, and the terms to come are the victor's to set.

variants.headline: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is ended
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is ended, and it ended on its knees. It opened with proclamations and marches; it closed with a signature given in the stronger's chamber. Of the pride that lit it, only the record remains.

variants.headline: Our war with {{initiator}} ends in capitulation
body: The war {{initiator}} brought to our doors has closed in capitulation. One of the two nations now answers to the other; the direction of the answer will be plain in the terms, once the terms are published.

variants.headline: Our war with {{target}} is settled
body: We are informed that the peace concluded with {{target}} is sealed, and sealed with a capitulation. A hard instrument, this paper concedes; yet the sword is sheathed on both sides of the border, and that much is reason to be glad.

variants.headline: A peace with visible terms
body: A peace settlement has been recorded, and this one comes with its terms showing: {{count}} concessions in all, namely {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: The terms between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: Peace between {{initiator}} and {{target}}.
Concessions on the record: {{count}}.
Their names: {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: Who owes what in the peace with {{target}}?
body: The peace with {{target}} lists concessions by kind: {{concessions}}. Before the council draws up its next budget, the public should be able to tell a debt from a windfall. Let the negotiators print the terms in two columns: what we gave and what we got.

variants.headline: A peace with terms tonight
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have settled their war tonight. The peace carries {{count}} concessions on the record. The ink is drying. The counting has begun.

variants.headline: Peace on one front only
body: We have made our peace with {{settled}}. The war goes on elsewhere: {{remaining}} is still in the field against us, and the guns on those fronts have not stopped.

variants.headline: One account closes, others stay open
body: The settlement with {{settled}} closes one account and leaves the rest open. The wars against {{remaining}} continue. Watch the roads rather than the speeches: the regiments coming off the quiet front will be marched to the loud one, and where they land will say which enemy the council fears most.

variants.headline: Peace with {{settled}}
body: We are informed that peace has been concluded with {{settled}}, and that the guns on that front are quiet. We note with regret that the war with {{remaining}} goes forward, and we permit ourselves the hope that the same good sense will find it before another harvest is spent.

variants.headline: Bells for one front, drums for the others
body: The bells have rung for peace with {{settled}}, while we are still at war with {{remaining}}. At the rope yard, a wagoner listened until the bells stopped and then asked which load was his. Let the council tell the people still packing the wagons why the fighting goes on elsewhere.

variants.headline: We are at peace
body: No power stands at war with us today. The fighting that filled these pages has stopped, and the counting of what it all cost has begun.

variants.headline: The record of rest
body: It is set down that in this season the fighting ceased, and the nation lay at rest from its enemies. The shrines filled past their doors, and the priests gave thanks. May the entry stand unamended a long while.

variants.headline: The long walk home
body: The first uniforms came up the road at noon, and the baker handed out the morning's loaves for nothing. Children ran alongside, dogs behind them. The war was signed away in some chancery; on the market square it ended at noon, with free bread.

variants.headline: Peace, and what to do with it
body: The guns are quiet, and this paper is glad of it. The work the silence leaves is plain: mend what the armies broke, pay what the armies borrowed, and find work for the men the armies took. Peace that only celebrates is peace half kept.

variants.headline: Please print the names by village
body: Madam, we hear that the war is over. If you learn who is coming home, please print the names by village. Our mother knows the name of ours by sight. It is the only word she can read, and she will want to find it for herself.

variants.headline: {{count}} of our companies lost in action
body: Our forces lost {{count}} companies in the recent fighting, every one of them to the same enemy power.

variants.headline: Our losses, counted
body: Companies lost in the recent fighting: {{count}}.
All to one and the same enemy.
The bill is public; the reply is not.

variants.headline: The empty bunks
body: {{count}} companies gone in the recent fighting, all to the same enemy. The landlady by the barracks gate stopped setting out the extra plates on Thursday. The town knew the number before the printer did.

variants.headline: The count from the fighting
body: They say {{count}} of our companies fell in the late fighting, and all of them to one enemy. The tellers agree on the number. When tellers agree, the news is not good.

variants.headline: Vassals drawn into the war
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has drawn in the vassal powers: {{vassals}}. Their banners now march under another's orders.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: What the vassals add
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has gained a supporting cast: {{vassals}}. A vassal's soldiers go where the master points, so every banner on that list is arithmetic for one side only. The war did not grow wider; it grew heavier.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: The record of vassalage honored
body: It is set down that {{vassals}} entered the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, being bound by vassalage. Their banners follow where the master's points, as such banners have always done, in this reign as in the ones before it.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Small kings, big wars
body: The quarrel of {{initiator}} and {{target}} now marches {{vassals}} to the front, none of them asked their view and none of them paid to have one. When the great quarrel, the small bleed. Citizens, note how these arrangements are made, and note who never appears in them.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Our advantage over {{opponent}} stops growing
body: Our advantage over {{opponent}} has stopped growing. At one supply yard the men are still loading flour each morning, and a baker who has filled the same order since the army went out says he has been asked what he can spare for another delivery.

variants.headline: The stalled advance against {{opponent}}
body: The tally in the war against {{opponent}} has scarcely moved in recent reports, after showing a clear advantage earlier. At a supply yard, a teamster waiting for his next load is asking whether he'll take it to the same camp. Another advance may change the tally. The teamsters still have to hitch up in the morning.

variants.byline: A farmer with a son in the ranks
variants.headline: The war that stands still
body: Madam, the war with {{opponent}} has stopped where it stood, and my son's regiment with it. The ploughing does not wait, the taxes do not wait, and the war alone has decided to wait. Will some counselor set down in plain words what the standing still is for?

variants.headline: Stuck: the war with {{opponent}}
body: The push we were promised hasn't moved in weeks. Same bills. Same map. Wars that stop moving don't stop charging.

variants.headline: Two friends go to war
body: {{first}} and {{second}} have gone to war with each other. Both are friends of ours, and each friendship stands on its own footing. Nothing in either one bound them to keep the peace with the other.

variants.headline: When friends fight
body: The war between {{first}} and {{second}} sets our two friendships against each other. Trade with both and arm neither, and each will count the even hand a slight. Neutrality between friends is a policy with no friends in it.

variants.headline: A plea in the war of {{first}} and {{second}}
body: We confess a heavy heart. {{first}} and {{second}}, both dear to this nation, have taken up arms against each other. Our wish is plain, and we state it without ornament: let our good offices be offered to both, and let the quarrel end at a table while both sides still have chairs.

variants.headline: They say the table is broken
body: It is told in the evenings that {{first}} and {{second}}, whose envoys drank from one cup beneath our roof, have crossed swords. The old ties, they say, snap loudest. The cup is still on the shelf. Nobody at the table will look at it.

variants.headline: The war runs long
body: The war has lasted {{turns}} turns. A carpenter who sent off two apprentices at the start says he has stopped promising customers that either man will be back in time to finish their doors.

variants.headline: The long stretch of the war with {{opponent}}
body: The war with {{opponent}} has run {{turns}} turns. Duration is itself a fact: armies age, treasuries thin, and the aims a war began with are quietly renegotiated by every season it survives. The original bill is never the final one.

variants.headline: The record of a long war
body: It is set down that the war has stood {{turns}} turns. Wars of this length were once the business of grandfathers. The record keeps such entries, and keeps them without joy.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} turns old
body: The war with {{opponent}} turned {{turns}} turns old this week. The bakery that used to count the days in its window has given up, and nobody under the awning remembers what the first week was about. Everyone remembers who is still over there.

variants.headline: The nation is at war
body: The nation has gone to war. The call to arms is out, the frontier watches are doubled, and these pages will follow the fighting turn by turn, wherever it runs.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: {{initiator}} has attacked
body: War tonight. {{initiator}} has declared war on us. Our forces are standing to their posts. The reserves are being counted. More bulletins as we have them.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: Hear it! {{initiator}} makes war on us
body: Word from the frontier: {{initiator}} has declared war on us! To arms, and mind the stores! {{initiator}} has made war on us, and the nation answers!{{hostileAllies}}

variants.headline: A state of war with {{target}}
body: We are informed that a state of war now exists between the nation and {{target}}. The government's decision, we are assured, was weighed long before it was made. This paper presumes the weighing was sound, and expects the case to be laid before the people while the armies are still within a day's march of home.{{hostileAllies}}

variants.when: role === 'joined' && reason === 'pact' && initiator !== null && target !== null
variants.headline: Their quarrel, our treaty
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is now ours by treaty. Pacts are signed in calm years and honored in hard ones; that is their worth and their price. Citizens, we are owed an accounting of what the paying buys, and we should ask for it now, while the ledgers are still open.{{hostileAllies}}

values.attackers: (() => { const declarations = new Map(merge.members.map(({ incident }) => [incident.initiator.id, incident.initiator])); const named = [...declarations.values()].filter(p => p.knows('name')).map(p => p.name); const unknown = declarations.size - named.length; if (unknown) named.push(unknown === 1 ? 'one unnamed power' : unknown + ' unnamed powers'); return named.join(', '); })()
values.otherFronts: (() => { const declarations = merge.members.map(m => m.incident); const fresh = new Set(declarations.map(i => i.initiator.id)); const first = declarations.reduce((a, b) => b.turn < a.turn ? b : a); const earlier = new Set(first.earlierWarOpponents.map(entry => entry.player.id)); const ongoing = [], other = []; for (const rival of self.wars) { if (!rival.knows('major') || !rival.major || !rival.knows('id') || fresh.has(rival.id)) continue; (earlier.has(rival.id) ? ongoing : other).push(rival.knows('name') ? rival.name : 'an unnamed power'); } return [ongoing.length ? 'Already at war with: ' + ongoing.join(', ') + '.' : '', other.length ? 'Other active fronts: ' + other.join(', ') + '.' : ''].filter(Boolean).join(' ') || 'These declarations account for all active major fronts.'; })()
values.allies: (() => { const named = new Map(); for (const { incident } of merge.members) for (const entry of incident.hostileCityStateAllies) if (entry.player.knows('name')) named.set(entry.player.id, entry.player.name); return named.size ? ' Hostile city-state allies: ' + [...named.values()].join(', ') + '.' : ''; })()

variants.headline: War on {{count}} fronts
body: New declarations of war: {{merge.values.attackers}}.{{merge.values.allies}}
{{merge.values.otherFronts}}

variants.headline: War on {{count}} fronts
body: The nation is at war with {{enemies}}. What was one quarrel is now several, and every front draws on the same purse and the same recruits.

variants.headline: Count the fronts
body: We are at war on {{count}} fronts, against {{enemies}}. Every soldier sent to one is a soldier the others go without, and the government has yet to say which front it means to win. A nation that means to win them all has not yet chosen.

variants.headline: Hear it! The nation fights on {{count}} fronts
body: Hear the roll of our enemies: {{enemies}}! The war is wide, and the harvest must be wide with it. Keep the fields tended and the watch set. Our enemies: {{enemies}}! The nation stands!

variants.headline: We are at war with {{count}} powers now
body: Enemy count: {{count}}. Names: {{enemies}}. Your bread, your sons, your taxes. Every front bills the same house.

variants.headline: The war tally favors {{opponent}}
body: The war tally against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}, well in their favor. A printer who posts each new count in his window says people have started asking when there might be talks.

variants.headline: The number nobody in the council quotes
body: The tally against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}, and no minister has said a word about it in a fortnight. A number that far below even is not misfortune; it is a description of how the fighting has gone. The country can bear the truth, and it is owed one.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} tonight
body: The war with {{opponent}} tonight. The running tally stands at {{score}} against us. Our commanders speak of holding. Nobody speaks of advancing.

variants.headline: The record of a hard season
body: It is set down that in the war with {{opponent}} the tally stands at {{score}} against us. Our fathers knew such seasons; the record keeps them, and does not flatter them. This entry joins that column.

variants.headline: Our side leads in the war with {{opponent}}
body: The tally against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}} in our favor. A woman collecting letters for the regiment says soldiers' families keep asking whether a better tally means their men will get home any sooner.

variants.headline: What the lead is worth
body: The tally against {{opponent}} has reached {{score}}. A lead of that size is earned in the field, but wars do not end on a ledger; they end when the other side decides the price is beyond paying. The number says we can begin asking.

variants.headline: The war proceeds favorably
body: Notice is given that the war with {{opponent}} proceeds favorably, the tally standing at {{score}} in the nation's favor. The councils may take satisfaction in the conduct of the arms; this paper takes some in the recording of it.

variants.headline: Good news, and the bill beside it
body: The war tally against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}, and the barkeep chalked it beside the price of a pint. A customer asked if a big enough score would pay his slate. "Try bringing coins," the keeper said, and poured him another.

variants.headline: The war sits lighter on the country
body: Weariness with the war has fallen to {{weariness}}, back below the halfway mark. In the shops, people have begun to ask what roof tiles and seed cost again.

variants.headline: Weariness eases in the war with {{opponent}}
body: We are informed that the public weariness over the war with {{opponent}} has eased to {{weariness}}. The nation breathes more evenly, and this paper notes the improvement with quiet satisfaction; a patient nation, history suggests, makes the better peacemaker.

variants.headline: The number behind the mood
body: Weariness with the war against {{opponent}} is down to {{weariness}}, from above the halfway mark. Tiredness does not win wars, but it can lose them. The patience the country has just recovered is worth more than a battle: it is what keeps a nation willing to pay for the next one.

variants.headline: Down to {{weariness}}: the country exhales
body: Still at war. The barber says it was nearly noon before anybody asked about the front. First complaint of the day: he'd taken too much off the back.

variants.headline: The war begins to wear us down
body: The latest weariness figure for the war with {{opponent}} is {{weariness}}. A cobbler says customers who once ordered a new pair now bring in boots he's already soled twice and ask him for one more season.

variants.headline: A weary nation, and no statement
body: Weariness with the war against {{opponent}} stands at {{weariness}}, past the halfway mark. The council has offered no statement on what the number is to be answered with, and we are obliged to observe that the silence is itself a statement.

variants.headline: Tired of the war? Say it plainly
body: The war with {{opponent}} has run long enough that the country's patience is being measured, and the measure is {{weariness}}. That number is a verdict forming in the streets. Councilors, read it before it hardens into something that can no longer be read.

variants.headline: The record of a weary nation
body: It is set down that the nation's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} stands at {{weariness}}. Long wars tire the patient. The record has said so in other reigns, and says so again in ours.
